resources.string: Used to capture screenshots via Quick Settings tile
SnapTile uses an accessibility service only to take screenshots when you tap the Quick Settings tile. No other data is collected.
SnapTile uses an accessibility service to carry out the action of its Quick Settings tile. Nothing else is read and no data is collected.
SnapTile takes screenshots cleanly via an accessibility service (no screen-recording prompt). Turn it on once under Accessibility → SnapTile.
Turn off for banking / UPI apps

Bank and UPI apps warn about any enabled third-party accessibility service, even one like SnapTile that only takes screenshots. It is now off, so those warnings stop. The tile still captures — Android asks for screen-capture consent each time. Turn it back on above for prompt-free capture.
Accessibility turned off. Re-enable it any time from this screen.
Turn SnapTile off under Accessibility settings

Tap the tile and the shot is taken at once. No prompt and no consent dialog, which is what lets SnapTile snip a region and open the paint editor. Needs SnapTile\'s accessibility service switched on — and banks and UPI apps warn about any enabled accessibility service, so they will warn about this one.

Android\'s own capture consent, the way any screen recorder works. No accessibility service is needed, so banking and UPI apps stay quiet. Android asks before each capture, so it is one extra tap every time.
Legacy method on. SnapTile\'s accessibility service is now off, so banking and UPI apps stop warning.
Native method on. Turn on SnapTile\'s accessibility service to use it.
Turn on SnapTile\'s accessibility service below. It is what the native capture method uses, and Android only lets you enable it, never the app itself.

SnapTile captures through an accessibility service so it can take the shot without Android\'s screen-recording prompt. That service has to be switched on by you — Android does not allow an app to enable it for itself.
SnapTile\'s accessibility service is off, so the native method cannot capture yet. Turn it on below, or switch SnapTile to the Legacy method on the main screen.
SnapTile\'s accessibility service is on ✓ — the native method is ready.
If the SnapTile switch is greyed out

On Android 13 and newer, Android hides this switch for apps that were installed outside a store. It is Android\'s rule for side-loaded apps, not something SnapTile can ask for at install time. Two taps fix it for good.
Tap ALLOW RESTRICTED SETTINGS below. Android opens SnapTile\'s App info page.
Tap the three dots (⋮) at the top right there.
Tap "Allow restricted settings", then come back and turn on SnapTile under Accessibility.
